title: Sedation Vacation in the ICU -- Introduction
content: The intensive care unit (ICU) admits the hospital’s most critically ill and unstable patients who require accelerated and concentrated care. Approximately 33% of ICU admissions involve respiratory failure from various causes, with many patients requiring intubation and mechanical ventilatory support. Continuous sedation forms a key component of care for these patients, aiming to reduce pain and anxiety, decrease oxygen consumption and the body’s stress response, prevent patient-ventilator asynchrony, minimize adverse neurocognitive effects, eg, depression and posttraumatic stress disorder, reduce ventilator-associated complications, including pneumonia and tracheostomy, and facilitate nursing care.

title: Sedation Vacation in the ICU -- Introduction
content: Mechanically ventilated patients often experience pain from endotracheal tubes, suctioning, indwelling catheters, surgical incisions, and frequent repositioning. [1] Sedation and analgesia are achieved using medications including benzodiazepines (eg, diazepam, lorazepam, and midazolam), opioid analgesics (eg, fentanyl, hydromorphone, morphine, and remifentanil), propofol, dexmedetomidine, ketamine, and antipsychotics (eg, haloperidol, quetiapine, and ziprasidone). No single agent has demonstrated superiority in efficacy or mortality benefit, though the Society of Critical Care Medicine recommends minimizing benzodiazepine use due to evidence of prolonged intubation. Sedative selection relies on clinical assessment, hemodynamic status, and a careful evaluation of risk-benefit profiles for each patient.

title: Sedation Vacation in the ICU -- Introduction
content: Continuous sedation has been associated with longer intubation times, extended ICU stays, impaired neurological assessment, increased delirium, and suppressed EEG activity, correlating with higher 6-month mortality. Evidence supports daily, short-term cessation of sedation, or “sedation vacations,” to evaluate the ongoing need for sedation, titrate medications appropriately, and assess neurological status. [2] Daily sedation interruptions reduce mechanical ventilation duration, ICU stay length, ventilator-associated infections, and the need for diagnostic tests related to oversedation. [3] [4]

title: Sedation Vacation in the ICU -- Introduction
content: A study conducted in 80 patients revealed that a daily sedation vacation protocol in patients with intravenous sedation reduced the incidence of ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP); therefore, this protocol was recommended as a preventative measure for VAP. [5] Furthermore, a randomized controlled trial in infants and children concluded that a sedation and ventilation weaning protocol significantly shortened the time to extubation compared to standard care. [6]

title: Sedation Vacation in the ICU -- Introduction
content: Sedation vacations first emerged in 2000 through a study by J.P. Kress et al, establishing spontaneous-awakening trials as a standard ICU practice to facilitate ventilator weaning. The study of spontaneous-awakening trials showed that daily sedation interruptions improved the time to extubation of 64 patients by approximately 2 days, which reduced the total admission time in the ICU by 3.5 days. Subsequent trials, including the 2008 Awakening and Breathing Controlled trial (“Wake Up and Breathe” protocol) and the 2010 No Sedation in ICU Patients trial, reinforced these findings, demonstrating that structured protocols for sedation interruption and spontaneous breathing trials significantly reduce ventilator-dependent days and ICU admission duration compared to unstructured approaches or continuous sedation. [7] [8] [9] [10]

title: Sedation Vacation in the ICU -- Issues of Concern
content: Sedation vacations can sometimes lead to complications that require careful monitoring and prompt intervention. Upon cessation of sedation, patients may have no recollection of being intubated and may be unaware of the multiple tubes and lines in place. Awakening can provoke confusion, anxiety, and agitation, placing both the patient and healthcare staff at risk. Furthermore, patients may attempt to remove endotracheal tubes or other invasive lines, potentially causing laryngeal injury or edema. If not addressed promptly, these events can lead to respiratory failure and, in severe cases, death. Additionally, heightened anxiety following sedation interruption can trigger a strong sympathetic response, resulting in tachycardia and elevated blood pressure. In older adults, elevated blood pressure increases the risk of stroke or myocardial infarction. [11] [12]

title: Sedation Vacation in the ICU -- Issues of Concern
content: Despite robust evidence supporting sedation vacations, adherence to this practice remains suboptimal in many ICUs. [13] Barriers include knowledge gaps, limited time, and insufficient staff to manage patients during awakening safely. Effective implementation relies on interprofessional care coordination, ongoing staff education, and adequate staffing, ensuring safe and consistent application of daily sedation vacation protocols. [14]

title: Sedation Vacation in the ICU -- Clinical Significance -- Sedation Vacation Assessments
content: Sedation vacation requires careful titration of sedative medications to achieve agitation-free, comfortable sedation at the lowest effective dose. Dosing must be individualized, as patient-specific factors, disease processes, and medication tolerances influence both the dose and choice of sedative. Two primary assessment tools guide sedation vacation management: the Riker Sedation-Agitation Scale (SAS) and the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS). [15] These scales quantify mental status, providing objective measures to determine whether sedation can be safely reduced or discontinued. SAS scores range from 1, representing an unarousable state, to 7, indicating dangerous agitation or combativeness, while a score of 4 indicates a calm, cooperative patient. RASS uses a similar spectrum, with -5 representing unarousable, 0 representing alert and calm, and +4 representing dangerously agitated or combative. Baseline mental status is further evaluated by the patient’s ability to follow commands, eg, eye tracking, hand squeezing, or tongue protrusion. [16] [17]

title: Sedation Vacation in the ICU -- Clinical Significance -- Sedation Vacation Readiness Assessment
content: Evidence-based protocols, eg, the Wake-Up and Breathe protocol, combine spontaneous awakening trials with spontaneous breathing trials to assess readiness for extubation in a stepwise manner. [18] Patient safety must be evaluated before attempting a spontaneous awakening trial, including screening for active seizures, alcohol withdrawal, profound agitation, paralytic use, myocardial ischemia, or elevated intracranial pressure. The presence of any of these contraindications necessitates postponing the trial and reevaluation within 24 hours. Failure markers during sedation interruption include agitation per SAS or RASS scales, pain, respiratory rate greater than 35 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation below 88%, respiratory distress, or acute cardiac arrhythmias. In such cases, sedatives should be resumed at 50% of the previous dose, followed by reassessment within 24 hours.

title: Sedation Vacation in the ICU -- Clinical Significance -- Sedation Vacation Failure Markers
content: Following a successful awakening trial, a spontaneous breathing trial can be initiated if patients demonstrate no agitation, oxygen saturation above 88%, FiO 2 below 50%, PEEP under 8 cm H 2 O, minimal vasopressor support, absence of myocardial ischemia, and adequate inspiratory effort. Failure markers for spontaneous breathing trials include respiratory rate outside 8 to 35 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation below 88%, respiratory distress, mental status changes, or cardiac arrhythmia. If none are present, extubation may proceed. Patients intubated for more than 48 hours without a cuff leak may receive steroids 4 to 5 hours before and 4 to 5 hours after extubation to reduce the risk of laryngeal edema and reintubation. [19]

title: Sedation Vacation in the ICU -- Clinical Significance -- Sedation Vacation Failure
content: When sedation vacation or breathing trials fail, the underlying cause must be addressed. Agitation or delirium may require antipsychotics, anxiety may respond to anxiolytics, and pain can be managed with low-dose opioid infusions or patches along with scheduled non-opioid analgesics. Dexmedetomidine effectively controls delirium and agitation without suppressing respiratory drive, allowing extubation while the infusion continues. Clinicians should also consider home medications; patients on chronic anxiolytics, antipsychotics, or pain management regimens should continue these medications while sedated or resume them promptly to prevent withdrawal. [12]

title: Sedation Vacation in the ICU -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Mechanically ventilated patients frequently experience discomfort from intubation, surgical procedures, and prolonged immobilization, necessitating continuous intravenous sedation and analgesia. Evidence-based practice recommends daily sedation vacations to assess neurological status, evaluate the ongoing need for sedation, and optimize ventilator weaning. Implementing this practice has been shown to reduce the duration of mechanical ventilation, decrease ICU length of stay, and lower the risk of ventilator-associated pneumonia, ultimately improving patient-centered outcomes and safety.

title: Sedation Vacation in the ICU -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Successful implementation of sedation vacation protocols requires coordinated interprofessional collaboration. Physicians, advanced practitioners, and general practitioners assess patient readiness and determine the appropriateness of sedation interruption and extubation. Nurses and respiratory therapists play critical roles in daily monitoring, executing sedation vacations, and supporting spontaneous awakening and breathing trials. Pharmacists contribute by selecting and titrating sedative and analgesic agents based on patient-specific factors. Clear communication, structured institutional protocols, and frequent team education facilitate consistency in practice, enhance patient safety, and optimize team performance. Daily ventilator rounds, safety assessments, and coordinated interventions ensure that patients undergo sedation vacations and weaning trials effectively, promoting faster recovery and improved ICU outcomes.

title: Sedation Vacation in the ICU -- Nursing, Allied Health, and Interprofessional Team Monitoring
content: Nursing staff should monitor for hemodynamic instability or profound changes in hemodynamics upon awakening, seizures, and severe agitation that is not controlled despite redirection or pharmacologic interventions. The presence of these should be considered a failure of the sedation vacation and spontaneous awakening trial, prompting the reinitiation of sedation. Based on the institute's protocols, the interprofessional team can reevaluate the appropriateness and safety of sedation vacation for the next day.
